Lancet 2000; 355: 1041–7. 650 Antineoplastics Carcinoid syndrome. Carcinoid tumours (also known as gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumours) occur mainly in the gastrointestinal tract or lungs (bronchi), al- though they occasionally arise in other organs with a com- mon embryological origin. Although they are relatively common, accounting for about 30% of all small bowel tu- mours, symptomatic carcinoid syndrome is rare, both be- cause the tumours vary in their behaviour depending on their embryological origin and because the liver is capable of metabolising those tumour products which are secreted into the portal circulation; only if the carcinoid tumour se- cretes into the systemic circulation, notably after metasta- sis to the liver, do symptoms occur. Tumours of embryo- logical fore-gut origin, usually found in the lung or stomach, predominantly secrete histamine or serotonin (5- HT); mid-gut tumours, with a usual primary site in the small intestine, are the most likely to metastasise and pro- duce carcinoid syndrome, and predominantly secrete sero- tonin; hind-gut tumours, in the distal colon or rectum, are commonly benign, and do not secrete active substances. The characteristic symptoms of carcinoid syndrome in- clude episodic flushing of the face and upper trunk (which may be provoked by alcohol, food, or stress), secretory di- arrhoea, wheezing and dyspnoea, weight loss, pellagra, painful hepatomegaly, and right-sided valvular heart dis- ease, which sometimes progresses to right heart failure and death.3,4 The management of carcinoid tumours usually involves surgical resection,3,4 and this can be curative, particularly if the primary tumour has not metastasised.2,5-7 Antineo- plastic chemotherapy has limited benefit,2,5 except per- haps in patients with atypical variants of
